raw_affiliation_strings: V. LEE HAMILTON is a professor of sociology at the University of Maryland, College Park. She received her Ph.D. in social psychology in 1975 from Harvard University where she worked with Herbert Kelman. Their 1989 book, Crimes of Obedience, focused on how citizens judge the responsibility of others who carry out acts of destructive obedience (such as the My Lai massacre in Vietnam). Hamilton also has co-authored a second book, Everyday Justice, which deals with responsibility judgments. Her current research interests include authority and obedience, responsibility attribution, and the relationship between self-blame and mental health. She is presently drafting a book on the mental health impact of recent auto plant closings on workers

raw_affiliation_strings: JOSEPH SANDERS received a Ph.D. in sociology and J.D. from Northwestern University. Presently, he is a professor of law at the University of Houston. He is the co-author of several books, including Everyday Justice, Invitation to Law and Social Science, and Social Science in Court: Mobilizing Experts in the School Desegregation Cases, and has written numerous social scientific and law review articles. His major current research interests include the attribution of responsibility for wrongdoing in hierarchies and the issue of products liability in tort law

raw_affiliation_strings: ROBERT R. HOLT is Professor of Psychology Emeritus and Director of the Program in Peace and Global Policy Studies at New York University. He was formerly Director of the Psychological Staff at the Menninger Foundation, and Director of the Research Center for Mental Health at NYU. His publications include Freud Reappraised, Methods in Clinical Psychology, and “Can Psychology Meet Einstein's Challenge?” in Political Psychology. His current research interests are in psychic numbing, metaphysical assumptions underlying operational codes and security policies, and the measurement and correlates of “new political thinking” and systems thinking

raw_affiliation_strings: BARRY E. COLLINS was a student of Donald Campbell's. He received his Ph.D. in social psychology in 1963 and was an assistant professor at Yale University. Since 1966, he has been at the University of California, Los Angeles. His books include Social Psychology, Social Psychology of Group Processes for Decision Making (co-authored with Harold Guetzkow), and Attitude Change: A Critical Analysis of Theoretical Approaches (co-authored with Chuck Kiesler and Norman Miller). For a short period in the 1970s, JSI published individual articles. He was editor for that section of the journal. Most recently, he has been interested in self and social-identity images as causes of behavior and in the application of these images to an understanding of obedience and AIDS-related behaviors

raw_affiliation_strings: DIANA E. BRIEF received her M.A. in psychology in 1992 and is currently a doctoral student in measurement and psychometrics at the University of California, Los Angeles. Her publications include “A Profile of Personality for a Russian Sample: As Indicated by the Comrey Personality Scales” and “The Comrey Personality Scales in Russian: A Study of Concurrent, Predictive, and External Validity.” She has presented several papers that concern observers' reactions to destructive obedience and has contributed, through her participation in the 1992 Conference on Psychology in the C.I.S., to the making of government policies regarding the conduct of American-Russian, cross-national research
